statement: A rectangular garden measures $12$ meters by $20$ meters. A path of uniform width $2$ meters runs all the way around the outside of the garden. What is the area of the path, in square meters?

choices.misconception: I added the width 2 only once to each dimension, so I used a 14 by 22 outer rectangle: 308 - 240 = 68.
I found the outer rectangle is 16 by 24 and then computed its perimeter, 2(16) + 2(24) = 80, instead of an area.
I multiplied the garden's perimeter 64 by the width 2 to get 128, then subtracted the four 2 by 2 corners, thinking they had been counted twice.
I multiplied the garden's perimeter 64 by the width 2 and forgot the four 2 by 2 corner squares.

hints: Find the area of everything, garden plus path, first.
The path is what is left when you remove the garden from the larger outer rectangle. Remember the path adds its width on both ends of each side.
The outer rectangle is $(12+4)$ by $(20+4)$, that is $16$ by $24$. Subtract the garden's $12 \cdot 20$.

solutions.reliable: The path adds $2$ meters on each end of each dimension, so the outer rectangle is $16$ by $24$, with area $384$. The garden itself has area $12 \cdot 20 = 240$. The path is the difference: $384 - 240 = 144$. Check by pieces: two strips $20 \times 2$, two strips $12 \times 2$ and four corner squares $2 \times 2$ give $80 + 48 + 16 = 144$. The transferable idea: the area of a border is the outer area minus the inner area.
solutions.elegant: A border of width $w$ has area $w$ times the perimeter measured along its centerline. The centerline is a $14$ by $22$ rectangle with perimeter $72$, and $72 \cdot 2 = 144$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
